1	---
2	title: "FigJam Type - User Flow"
3	description: "A person's path through a product composed as a FigJam board: four shapes, labelled exits, colour by kind, optional zones and a nine-node budget."
4	contextType: implementation
5	importance_tier: important
6	trigger_phrases:
7	  - "figjam user flow"
8	  - "user flow rules"
9	  - "screen flow figjam"
10	  - "merge dot"
11	version: 1.0.5.0
12	---
13	
14	# FigJam Type - User Flow
15	
16	A user flow is the screens and choices one person passes through to reach a goal. It is the default Flow type and the strictest, because it is drawn from screenshots and frames a reader will compare node by node.
17	
18	**Loading Condition:** CONDITIONAL, when the Flow route draws a user flow
19	**Purpose:** The grammar, rules, budget and read-back for a user flow
20	**Pairs With:** `assets/flow-templates.md`
21	
22	---
23	
24	## 1. WHEN TO USE
25	
26	**The reader's question:** which screens does a person pass through, and where do they choose?
27	
28	- A flow drawn from screenshots, from Figma frames or from a product doc that walks one person through the product
29	- A platform split, such as desktop and mobile, that rejoins on a later screen
30	- A journey, which Flow Mode does not draw as such, redrawn as the screens it visits
31	
32	Use another type when several people or teams hand work to each other (a process), when the subject is services and stores (an architecture) or when time order between systems is the point (a sequence).
33	
34	---
35	
36	## 2. WHAT THE BOARD DRAWS
37	
38	`flowchart LR` or `flowchart TD`, composed into a board as Section 6 sets out. No `%% type:` line is needed, because a flowchart with none is a user flow.
39	
40	| Shape | Mermaid | Means |
41	|---|---|---|
42	| Stadium | `id([Label])` | The flow starts or ends here |
43	| Rectangle | `id[Label]` | A screen or an action |
44	| Rhombus | `id{Label?}` | A choice, written as a question |
45	| Circle | `id((.))` | A merge dot, where branches rejoin, with no words |
46	
47	Every connector is a solid one-way arrow, `-->`, with an optional label: `a -->|Yes| b`.
48	
49	On the board the first screen takes the `entry` role, every other screen the `neutral` role, a decision a diamond in the `decision` role, the goal the `goal` role and every other end the `exit` role, beside the main line rather than on it, and `assets/figjam-design.md` names the swatch each role draws. The main route from the first screen to the goal runs on one straight line, and `%% zone:` lines group the screens into named stages, as `assets/flow-templates.md` Section 1 sets out.
50	
51	Every move carries an actor in the model, one of a person, a system or a timer. A system step is marked automatic and a timer step is fired by time, so neither is ever counted as a missing user action.
52	
53	---
54	
55	## 3. RULES
56	
57	The check enforces:
58	
59	- **Four shapes only.** No other shape, no subgraph and never a colour per type. A `%% zone:` line does the grouping instead
60	- **A decision has 1 to 3 exits, each labelled.** A fourth outcome means the decision is two decisions
61	- **Every node connected, every step with a way in and a way out.** Only a stadium starts or ends the flow, and a stadium never sits mid-flow. The first node may take a loop back to it
62	- **A merge dot carries no words**
63	- **Solid one-way arrows only.** A dotted, thick, headless or two-way connector would carry a second meaning. A proposal's status goes in its label, and a `%% goal:` line names the goal
64	- **Left to right or top to bottom,** the same way for every diagram of one flow. Left to right is the default, because the composer keeps the main route on one straight line across a board that reads wider than tall and sets each branch beside it. Top to bottom suits a short flow
65	- **Labels of at most 40 characters on one line,** in double quotes when they hold a parenthesis, a colon or a slash
66	- **camelCase ids,** never an underscore or a reserved word such as `end`
67	- **No emoji, markup or literal `\n`** anywhere in the block but a `%%` comment
68	- **At most 9 nodes,** and exactly one `style` line from `references/style-guide.md`
69	
70	Judged by hand:
71	
72	- **No node returns to itself.** A connector from a node back onto the same node draws no loop a reader can follow, so a retry goes into a label or through the node it returns through, and `scripts/flow_check.py` refuses one
73	- **Labels name the screen or the action in the product's own words,** one to four words where those words allow
74	- **A decision label is a question and each exit one of its answers**
75	- **Exits read the same way across the flow,** such as Yes to the right and No below, so a reader learns the pattern once
76	- **The shape carries the type, so the label does not repeat it.** Write `valid{Card valid?}`, never `valid{Decision: card valid?}`
77	- **A state is a screen in another condition, and no fifth shape carries it.** A state earns its own node only when a different action reaches it or a reader can be trapped in it, and otherwise the condition goes in the screen's label and under `Left out:`
78	
79	---
80	
81	## 4. BUDGET AND SPLITTING
82	
83	Nine nodes is sk-design-diagram's general budget and matches what a hand-drawn user flow uses. A longer flow splits into diagrams that hand off through a named end and a start with the same label, all in one file. When the user asked in so many words for one board, cut the lowest-priority part instead, name it under `Left out:` and offer the split as the alternative in the playback. Every source step lands in one diagram or under `Left out:`, never dropped silently. At `Meeting screen` distance labels drop to 32 characters. At `Wall` distance the budget drops to 6 nodes, with labels at 25 characters, as the reading distance dial in `references/flow-mode.md` Section 4 sets out.
84	
85	---
86	
87	## 5. COLOUR, ZONES AND NOTES
88	
89	The composer colours every screen by its kind. A user flow and a process each carry exactly one `style` line, which marks the first glance. A styled failing end or decision keeps its kind and takes the accent's outline. The goal is named by a `%% goal:` line rather than styled. A styled step is drawn in the accent's pair. The line marks meaning: on an end, in the light red pair, it marks a failure, and on a screen it puts that screen in focus, as `references/style-guide.md` Section 3 sets out. Zones are `%% zone:` lines in flow order, and once a flow has zones every screen sits in one. A note on a screen, such as a drop-off rate, goes on through the pins and legend recipe in `references/hybrid-workflow.md`.
90	
91	---
92	
93	## 6. WRITING THE BOARD
94	
95	`scripts/compose_board.py` composes the model and one `use_figma` call draws the board, as `references/flow-mode.md` Section 6 sets out. On the generated fallback, `generate_diagram` takes `name`, `mermaidSyntax` and `userIntent`, with `name` set to the flow and its hand-off and no `useArchitectureLayoutCode`. The `fj` route can also draw a user flow when neither hosted tool is connected.
96	
97	---
98	
99	## 7. READ-BACK
100	
101	Count on the board, against the model: nodes, connectors, decision exits labelled, every node label, and for each model connector a board connector joining the same two nodes in the same direction with the same label, following a routed edge through its legs as `references/flow-mode.md` Section 7 sets out. When the flow has zones, each screen sits in its zone.
102	
103	```text
104	Read-back: 8 of 8 nodes, 8 of 8 connectors, 2 of 2 decision exits labelled
105	```
106	
107	---
108	
109	## 8. PATTERNS AND EXAMPLE
110	
111	- `assets/flow-templates.md` holds five user-flow patterns that pass the check
112	- `assets/examples/user-flow-fernhouse-return.md` walks one flow from screenshots to the reply
113

---
title: "FigJam Type - User Flow"
description: "A person's path through a product composed as a FigJam board: four shapes, labelled exits, colour by kind, optional zones and a nine-node budget."
contextType: implementation
importance_tier: important
trigger_phrases:
  - "figjam user flow"
  - "user flow rules"
  - "screen flow figjam"
  - "merge dot"
version: 1.0.5.0
---

# FigJam Type - User Flow

A user flow is the screens and choices one person passes through to reach a goal. It is the default Flow type and the strictest, because it is drawn from screenshots and frames a reader will compare node by node.

**Loading Condition:** CONDITIONAL, when the Flow route draws a user flow
**Purpose:** The grammar, rules, budget and read-back for a user flow
**Pairs With:** `assets/flow-templates.md`

---

## 1. WHEN TO USE

**The reader's question:** which screens does a person pass through, and where do they choose?

- A flow drawn from screenshots, from Figma frames or from a product doc that walks one person through the product
- A platform split, such as desktop and mobile, that rejoins on a later screen
- A journey, which Flow Mode does not draw as such, redrawn as the screens it visits

Use another type when several people or teams hand work to each other (a process), when the subject is services and stores (an architecture) or when time order between systems is the point (a sequence).

---

## 2. WHAT THE BOARD DRAWS

`flowchart LR` or `flowchart TD`, composed into a board as Section 6 sets out. No `%% type:` line is needed, because a flowchart with none is a user flow.

| Shape | Mermaid | Means |
|---|---|---|
| Stadium | `id([Label])` | The flow starts or ends here |
| Rectangle | `id[Label]` | A screen or an action |
| Rhombus | `id{Label?}` | A choice, written as a question |
| Circle | `id((.))` | A merge dot, where branches rejoin, with no words |

Every connector is a solid one-way arrow, `-->`, with an optional label: `a -->|Yes| b`.

On the board the first screen takes the `entry` role, every other screen the `neutral` role, a decision a diamond in the `decision` role, the goal the `goal` role and every other end the `exit` role, beside the main line rather than on it, and `assets/figjam-design.md` names the swatch each role draws. The main route from the first screen to the goal runs on one straight line, and `%% zone:` lines group the screens into named stages, as `assets/flow-templates.md` Section 1 sets out.

Every move carries an actor in the model, one of a person, a system or a timer. A system step is marked automatic and a timer step is fired by time, so neither is ever counted as a missing user action.

---

## 3. RULES

The check enforces:

- **Four shapes only.** No other shape, no subgraph and never a colour per type. A `%% zone:` line does the grouping instead
- **A decision has 1 to 3 exits, each labelled.** A fourth outcome means the decision is two decisions
- **Every node connected, every step with a way in and a way out.** Only a stadium starts or ends the flow, and a stadium never sits mid-flow. The first node may take a loop back to it
- **A merge dot carries no words**
- **Solid one-way arrows only.** A dotted, thick, headless or two-way connector would carry a second meaning. A proposal's status goes in its label, and a `%% goal:` line names the goal
- **Left to right or top to bottom,** the same way for every diagram of one flow. Left to right is the default, because the composer keeps the main route on one straight line across a board that reads wider than tall and sets each branch beside it. Top to bottom suits a short flow
- **Labels of at most 40 characters on one line,** in double quotes when they hold a parenthesis, a colon or a slash
- **camelCase ids,** never an underscore or a reserved word such as `end`
- **No emoji, markup or literal `\n`** anywhere in the block but a `%%` comment
- **At most 9 nodes,** and exactly one `style` line from `references/style-guide.md`

Judged by hand:

- **No node returns to itself.** A connector from a node back onto the same node draws no loop a reader can follow, so a retry goes into a label or through the node it returns through, and `scripts/flow_check.py` refuses one
- **Labels name the screen or the action in the product's own words,** one to four words where those words allow
- **A decision label is a question and each exit one of its answers**
- **Exits read the same way across the flow,** such as Yes to the right and No below, so a reader learns the pattern once
- **The shape carries the type, so the label does not repeat it.** Write `valid{Card valid?}`, never `valid{Decision: card valid?}`
- **A state is a screen in another condition, and no fifth shape carries it.** A state earns its own node only when a different action reaches it or a reader can be trapped in it, and otherwise the condition goes in the screen's label and under `Left out:`

---

## 4. BUDGET AND SPLITTING

Nine nodes is sk-design-diagram's general budget and matches what a hand-drawn user flow uses. A longer flow splits into diagrams that hand off through a named end and a start with the same label, all in one file. When the user asked in so many words for one board, cut the lowest-priority part instead, name it under `Left out:` and offer the split as the alternative in the playback. Every source step lands in one diagram or under `Left out:`, never dropped silently. At `Meeting screen` distance labels drop to 32 characters. At `Wall` distance the budget drops to 6 nodes, with labels at 25 characters, as the reading distance dial in `references/flow-mode.md` Section 4 sets out.

---

## 5. COLOUR, ZONES AND NOTES

The composer colours every screen by its kind. A user flow and a process each carry exactly one `style` line, which marks the first glance. A styled failing end or decision keeps its kind and takes the accent's outline. The goal is named by a `%% goal:` line rather than styled. A styled step is drawn in the accent's pair. The line marks meaning: on an end, in the light red pair, it marks a failure, and on a screen it puts that screen in focus, as `references/style-guide.md` Section 3 sets out. Zones are `%% zone:` lines in flow order, and once a flow has zones every screen sits in one. A note on a screen, such as a drop-off rate, goes on through the pins and legend recipe in `references/hybrid-workflow.md`.

---

## 6. WRITING THE BOARD

`scripts/compose_board.py` composes the model and one `use_figma` call draws the board, as `references/flow-mode.md` Section 6 sets out. On the generated fallback, `generate_diagram` takes `name`, `mermaidSyntax` and `userIntent`, with `name` set to the flow and its hand-off and no `useArchitectureLayoutCode`. The `fj` route can also draw a user flow when neither hosted tool is connected.

---

## 7. READ-BACK

Count on the board, against the model: nodes, connectors, decision exits labelled, every node label, and for each model connector a board connector joining the same two nodes in the same direction with the same label, following a routed edge through its legs as `references/flow-mode.md` Section 7 sets out. When the flow has zones, each screen sits in its zone.

```text
Read-back: 8 of 8 nodes, 8 of 8 connectors, 2 of 2 decision exits labelled
```

---

## 8. PATTERNS AND EXAMPLE

- `assets/flow-templates.md` holds five user-flow patterns that pass the check
- `assets/examples/user-flow-fernhouse-return.md` walks one flow from screenshots to the reply

1	---
2	title: "FigJam Diagram Quality Rubric"
3	description: "The taste gate a FigJam model passes before the write gate, translated from sk-design-diagram's success criteria: type fit, the remove test, signal, the check, the board, the design rubric that scores a composed board and the reply."
4	contextType: implementation
5	importance_tier: important
6	trigger_phrases:
7	  - "figjam quality rubric"
8	  - "diagram taste gate"
9	  - "remove test"
10	  - "figjam review checklist"
11	  - "figjam design rubric"
12	version: 1.0.9.0
13	---
14	
15	# FigJam Diagram Quality Rubric
16	
17	The script checks what a script can see. This rubric is the rest: whether the diagram should exist, whether every node earns its place and whether the reader can trust what lands on the board. Walk it after the check passes and before the write gate.
18	
19	**Loading Condition:** CONDITIONAL, on every Flow route before the write gate
20	**Purpose:** The judgement pass between the pre-write check and the gate
21	**Scope:** The model, the provenance table, the planned extensions and, after the write, the board and the reply
22	
23	---
24	
25	## 1. TYPE FIT
26	
27	- [ ] The type answers the reader's question, as `references/flow-mode.md` Section 3 maps it
28	- [ ] A table, a list or a paragraph would not do the same job. If it would, say so and offer that instead
29	- [ ] The type's reference in `references/types/` was loaded and its judged-by-hand rules were applied
30	- [ ] A request for a kind Flow Mode does not draw was answered with the nearest type it does draw, or a plain no
31	
32	---
33	
34	## 2. THE REMOVE TEST
35	
36	sk-design-diagram's highest-quality move is usually deletion. A diagram is done when nothing can be removed.
37	
38	The remove test runs on the outline before the first Mermaid block, because a step cut from a list of steps costs a sentence and the same step cut from a drawn diagram costs a redraw. This section is the third rung of the challenge ladder in `references/flow-mode.md` Section 3, so the two rungs above it are asked first: what the board must not do, and whether a list, a table or a paragraph would serve the reader better.
39	
40	- [ ] The `userIntent` sentence was agreed in the sparring and is the first line of the outline, rather than composed at the write call
41	- [ ] The remove test ran on the outline, one line per node and edge, before any layout was judged
42	- [ ] An unanswered sparring proposal is marked assumed and named in the playback before the gate
43	- [ ] No node can be removed without the reader losing a step they need
44	- [ ] Every node serves the `userIntent` sentence, or it is cut and named under `Left out:`
45	- [ ] No two nodes always travel together. If they do, they are one node
46	- [ ] No connector restates what the layout already shows
47	- [ ] No label repeats what the shape already says
48	- [ ] No diagram carries the same label on four or more connectors. Cut them all, or keep one where the label says something the shape cannot. Decision exits and sequence messages are exempt, and an architecture renames each edge instead, as its type reference sets out
49	- [ ] The remove test ran on the outline before the first Mermaid block, so no node was drawn only to be cut
50	- [ ] The diagram sits inside its budget, or was split, and every cut is named under `Left out:`
51	
52	---
53	
54	## 3. SIGNAL
55	
56	The marked node is chosen against a target written down first. A board judged only against itself cannot catch a second focal object, such as a title that repeats the claim the marked node was meant to carry. Three lines are written before the first Mermaid block:
57	
58	1. **First glance.** The one claim, decision or object that should win within two seconds
59	2. **Second glance.** The evidence or relationship that advances it
60	3. **Last glance.** The risk, the metadata or the appendix that stays available without competing
61	
62	Those three lines travel into the gate, so the marked node is chosen from them and the reply can say what should win. After the first glance, filled shapes and their keyed fills outweigh connector labels and text in the overview, so the lines name a filled group such as the gray end states before the labels between them. Every node the board draws sits in one of the three lines, because a part the lines leave out still reads early and takes the second glance. Lanes and zones read as part of the frame, like the title block, so the lines plan the nodes inside them and never the lane or zone itself. On a user flow or a process a reader takes the main row after the accent, in path order whatever its fills. The main row is the longest path from the light blue entry to the goal, which the composer draws as one row, or across the lanes on a laned process, so a detour on that path is part of it. The second glance names the main row in path order, the entry included and the accented node left out, and the last glance names every node off it, such as an error, an exit, a branch, a loop back or a data store, in path order. The entry and the goal in one line carry no order between them. On any other type a gateway, an error and a critical bar carry a 4 pixel outline and read right after the accent, so the second glance line plans each one the board draws unless the accent sits on it. A revision that makes a changed end the second glance follows the revision rule below, and a state board takes its order from `references/types/state.md` Section 5 instead.
63	
64	- [ ] One accent on a user flow or a process, on the node a reader would keep if they could keep only one, never the node that comes first. A decision, a failure end and the one step in focus are the candidates. The goal never takes the accent, because the composer draws it at the far end of the main row, where readers reach it last whatever its outline, so a `%% goal:` line names it instead, as `references/style-guide.md` Section 3 sets out. Two that tie mean the diagram splits
65	- [ ] The three glance lines were written before the model and named in the gate
66	- [ ] On a user flow or a process the first glance is the accented node, marked by the one `style` line the check requires, and the gate names it. On a state board it is the first state, which the layout always shows first, and a `%% focus:` line marks the state the request names where it is drawn, as `references/types/state.md` Section 5 sets out. On any other type it is the node, message or task a `%% focus:` line names, or, when the model has none, whatever the layout shows first, and the gate says which. The first glance is one node, message or task, never a group such as the end states, and when the layout would show another first, a `%% focus:` line marks it, so the gate never promises a first glance the board does not show. Except on a state board, it is the claim the reader came for rather than the node the flow reaches first, and nothing the second or last glance owns competes with it
67	- [ ] On a revision the changed step, decision or failure end is the first glance and takes the accent. When the change is any other end, the accent stays on the decision or step the board already marks and the gate and the reply name the changed end alone as the second glance, with the entry, the decisions and the rest of the main row in the last glance line, because a style line on an end makes that end the goal and a second glance shared with the entry hides the change. On an extension that pins several problems, the accent stays where the board put it and the pins carry the problems as the second glance
68	- [ ] When the model gives a reason for the accent as `%% focus: <id> because <reason>`, as `references/style-guide.md` Section 3 sets out, the key's `In focus` entry carries that reason, so a reader who asks why one node is marked finds the answer on the board
69	- [ ] No title repeats the focal claim, so one idea carries one focal object. Where the title already states the claim, the marked node carries the evidence, the consequence or the next move
70	- [ ] The title names what the reader is looking at, the subtitle says in one sentence who reads it and why, and the source line names the sources and what was left out
71	- [ ] Shape and outline and label carry the meaning without colour, so the diagram reads in greyscale
72	- [ ] The key the composer draws names every kind, line and arrow the board shows and nothing else, and no note adds a second key beside it
73	- [ ] Every zone carries a name a reader can see, and zones group what belongs together rather than marking a position
74	- [ ] Every label uses the product's or the source's own words. Proper nouns are never renamed
75	- [ ] The naming fits the audience: exact component names for engineers, plain verbs for a mixed team, capabilities and outcomes for leadership
76	- [ ] Nothing was invented to fill a lane, a slot or a gap. A missing step is asked about or named, never guessed
77	
78	---
79	
80	## 4. PROVENANCE
81	
82	- [ ] Every node has a row in the provenance table naming its source and its source class
83	- [ ] Nothing marked proposal or unknown is drawn as current behavior. Its status sits in its label, or it is left out
84	- [ ] Every causal edge is stated by its sources from both ends. An edge one source states and another contradicts is a finding, not a connector
85	- [ ] A contradicted item leaves a trace the reader can see. It sits in the reply's `Left out:` line with both sources and the reason, or the one question that asks which source governs settled it. Nothing is removed in silence and no extra line is invented for it
86	
87	---
88	
89	## 5. THE CHECK AND THE GATE
90	
91	- [ ] `scripts/flow_check.py` printed `PASSED` for the model file, with the type each diagram was read as
92	- [ ] The measures printed beside the counts were read: the widest rank, the longest path, the connectors per step, the average label length and the crossing pairs, against the budgets `scripts/figjam_checks/layout.py` sets
93	- [ ] A measure out of band was fixed in the model rather than on the board and the check rerun after the change, because the composer owns the layout and a tangled shape is never rearranged after the write
94	- [ ] `scripts/compose_board.py` printed `COMPOSED` for every diagram, with the counts the read-back will look for
95	- [ ] The gate message names the plan, the file, what will be written, any planned extensions, the calls the write will spend and the rollback
96	- [ ] The gate showed the sketch with the check's result and answered the four critique questions `references/flow-mode.md` step 7 names, unless the user already settled them in this conversation
97	- [ ] On the generated fallback, an architecture call carries `useArchitectureLayoutCode`, and no other type carries it
98	
99	---
100	
101	## 6. THE BOARD
102	
103	After the write, before the reply:
104	
105	- [ ] The read-back counts match the model, as the type's reference sets them out
106	- [ ] Each provenance row whose class is not current behavior or whose edge is inferred was re-read against its source before the gate, and the row records the reason. A row that quotes a source line was not re-read
107	- [ ] The write returned no warning, and its counts match the counts the model expects
108	- [ ] The `COMPOSED` line named the design the board was drawn in, and each `DESIGN` warning it counted became a `Finding:` line naming the token and the shipped value the board used instead
109	- [ ] The overview is the screenshot the composing call returned, and `get_figjam` supplies the outline with a screenshot of each node
110	- [ ] A node that needs its own view is read with `get_screenshot` and a node id from that read, because the tool fails without one
111	- [ ] Two screenshots of the board were taken for this pass: one of the whole board in a single frame and one at 100% zoom. Composition is judged on the overview, because a crossing and a crowded label are invisible at reading size
112	- [ ] The overview reads in the order the model plans, and that order was written down before the first screenshot
113	- [ ] The overview shows no connector crossing another, no connector or label on a zone title, no two edges sharing a trunk the model draws apart and no two labels touching
114	- [ ] No edge runs through a zone it neither starts nor ends in. Edges that only arrive may share one magnet and then lie together for no more than 200 pixels
115	- [ ] One screenshot of the diagram shows no stretched shape, no label cut off and no overlap with existing board content
116	- [ ] Every gap a note or a person placed falls in one of the three bands `references/style-guide.md` Section 7 states, and two unrelated groups sit no closer than the text blocks inside a card
117	- [ ] Each zone holds its own nodes and no other, and no zone overlaps another
118	- [ ] The same screenshot shows no connector crossing and no edge that reads as joining the wrong node. Each edge is followed by eye from end to end, because a connector count does not prove that a route is clear
119	- [ ] Every colour on the board matches its entry in the key, the marked node sits where Section 3 places it, and the board answers the `userIntent` sentence without the model beside it
120	- [ ] Every fill on the board resolves to a role in the active design, as `assets/figjam-design.md` holds it, no zone tint shares a hue with a kind inside it or with the accent, and no note added a colour the design does not name
121	- [ ] The marked node reads first, and no other node competes with it, except on a state board, where it reads where the composer draws it and leads its glance line
122	- [ ] A screenshot finding is reported, and it is fixed only by reshaping the model and composing again after a yes, inside the two-attempt bound `references/flow-mode.md` Section 9 sets
123	- [ ] Each extension landed where planned and covers no composed node's label
124	- [ ] Nothing was moved, resized or restyled after the write
125	- [ ] Every finding below full marks names the label it sits on, where it sits in the frame, and one fix, which is a model change composed again after a yes or a named composer limit the writer cannot move
126	
127	---
128	
129	## 7. THE DESIGN RUBRIC
130	
131	The checklists above decide whether a board may ship. The design rubric scores how well it reads, so two boards of the same model, or a board before and after a change, can be compared on something firmer than a glance. Score the overview screenshot on nine criteria, each 0, 1 or 2, for a total out of 18. ---
title: "FigJam Diagram Quality Rubric"
description: "The taste gate a FigJam model passes before the write gate, translated from sk-design-diagram's success criteria: type fit, the remove test, signal, the check, the board, the design rubric that scores a composed board and the reply."
contextType: implementation
importance_tier: important
trigger_phrases:
  - "figjam quality rubric"
  - "diagram taste gate"
  - "remove test"
  - "figjam review checklist"
  - "figjam design rubric"
version: 1.0.9.0
---

# FigJam Diagram Quality Rubric

The script checks what a script can see. This rubric is the rest: whether the diagram should exist, whether every node earns its place and whether the reader can trust what lands on the board. Walk it after the check passes and before the write gate.

**Loading Condition:** CONDITIONAL, on every Flow route before the write gate
**Purpose:** The judgement pass between the pre-write check and the gate
**Scope:** The model, the provenance table, the planned extensions and, after the write, the board and the reply

---

## 1. TYPE FIT

- [ ] The type answers the reader's question, as `references/flow-mode.md` Section 3 maps it
- [ ] A table, a list or a paragraph would not do the same job. If it would, say so and offer that instead
- [ ] The type's reference in `references/types/` was loaded and its judged-by-hand rules were applied
- [ ] A request for a kind Flow Mode does not draw was answered with the nearest type it does draw, or a plain no

---

## 2. THE REMOVE TEST

sk-design-diagram's highest-quality move is usually deletion. A diagram is done when nothing can be removed.

The remove test runs on the outline before the first Mermaid block, because a step cut from a list of steps costs a sentence and the same step cut from a drawn diagram costs a redraw. This section is the third rung of the challenge ladder in `references/flow-mode.md` Section 3, so the two rungs above it are asked first: what the board must not do, and whether a list, a table or a paragraph would serve the reader better.

- [ ] The `userIntent` sentence was agreed in the sparring and is the first line of the outline, rather than composed at the write call
- [ ] The remove test ran on the outline, one line per node and edge, before any layout was judged
- [ ] An unanswered sparring proposal is marked assumed and named in the playback before the gate
- [ ] No node can be removed without the reader losing a step they need
- [ ] Every node serves the `userIntent` sentence, or it is cut and named under `Left out:`
- [ ] No two nodes always travel together. If they do, they are one node
- [ ] No connector restates what the layout already shows
- [ ] No label repeats what the shape already says
- [ ] No diagram carries the same label on four or more connectors. Cut them all, or keep one where the label says something the shape cannot. Decision exits and sequence messages are exempt, and an architecture renames each edge instead, as its type reference sets out
- [ ] The remove test ran on the outline before the first Mermaid block, so no node was drawn only to be cut
- [ ] The diagram sits inside its budget, or was split, and every cut is named under `Left out:`

---

## 3. SIGNAL

The marked node is chosen against a target written down first. A board judged only against itself cannot catch a second focal object, such as a title that repeats the claim the marked node was meant to carry. Three lines are written before the first Mermaid block:

1. **First glance.** The one claim, decision or object that should win within two seconds
2. **Second glance.** The evidence or relationship that advances it
3. **Last glance.** The risk, the metadata or the appendix that stays available without competing

Those three lines travel into the gate, so the marked node is chosen from them and the reply can say what should win. After the first glance, filled shapes and their keyed fills outweigh connector labels and text in the overview, so the lines name a filled group such as the gray end states before the labels between them. Every node the board draws sits in one of the three lines, because a part the lines leave out still reads early and takes the second glance. Lanes and zones read as part of the frame, like the title block, so the lines plan the nodes inside them and never the lane or zone itself. On a user flow or a process a reader takes the main row after the accent, in path order whatever its fills. The main row is the longest path from the light blue entry to the goal, which the composer draws as one row, or across the lanes on a laned process, so a detour on that path is part of it. The second glance names the main row in path order, the entry included and the accented node left out, and the last glance names every node off it, such as an error, an exit, a branch, a loop back or a data store, in path order. The entry and the goal in one line carry no order between them. On any other type a gateway, an error and a critical bar carry a 4 pixel outline and read right after the accent, so the second glance line plans each one the board draws unless the accent sits on it. A revision that makes a changed end the second glance follows the revision rule below, and a state board takes its order from `references/types/state.md` Section 5 instead.

- [ ] One accent on a user flow or a process, on the node a reader would keep if they could keep only one, never the node that comes first. A decision, a failure end and the one step in focus are the candidates. The goal never takes the accent, because the composer draws it at the far end of the main row, where readers reach it last whatever its outline, so a `%% goal:` line names it instead, as `references/style-guide.md` Section 3 sets out. Two that tie mean the diagram splits
- [ ] The three glance lines were written before the model and named in the gate
- [ ] On a user flow or a process the first glance is the accented node, marked by the one `style` line the check requires, and the gate names it. On a state board it is the first state, which the layout always shows first, and a `%% focus:` line marks the state the request names where it is drawn, as `references/types/state.md` Section 5 sets out. On any other type it is the node, message or task a `%% focus:` line names, or, when the model has none, whatever the layout shows first, and the gate says which. The first glance is one node, message or task, never a group such as the end states, and when the layout would show another first, a `%% focus:` line marks it, so the gate never promises a first glance the board does not show. Except on a state board, it is the claim the reader came for rather than the node the flow reaches first, and nothing the second or last glance owns competes with it
- [ ] On a revision the changed step, decision or failure end is the first glance and takes the accent. When the change is any other end, the accent stays on the decision or step the board already marks and the gate and the reply name the changed end alone as the second glance, with the entry, the decisions and the rest of the main row in the last glance line, because a style line on an end makes that end the goal and a second glance shared with the entry hides the change. On an extension that pins several problems, the accent stays where the board put it and the pins carry the problems as the second glance
- [ ] When the model gives a reason for the accent as `%% focus: <id> because <reason>`, as `references/style-guide.md` Section 3 sets out, the key's `In focus` entry carries that reason, so a reader who asks why one node is marked finds the answer on the board
- [ ] No title repeats the focal claim, so one idea carries one focal object. Where the title already states the claim, the marked node carries the evidence, the consequence or the next move
- [ ] The title names what the reader is looking at, the subtitle says in one sentence who reads it and why, and the source line names the sources and what was left out
- [ ] Shape and outline and label carry the meaning without colour, so the diagram reads in greyscale
- [ ] The key the composer draws names every kind, line and arrow the board shows and nothing else, and no note adds a second key beside it
- [ ] Every zone carries a name a reader can see, and zones group what belongs together rather than marking a position
- [ ] Every label uses the product's or the source's own words. Proper nouns are never renamed
- [ ] The naming fits the audience: exact component names for engineers, plain verbs for a mixed team, capabilities and outcomes for leadership
- [ ] Nothing was invented to fill a lane, a slot or a gap. A missing step is asked about or named, never guessed

---

## 4. PROVENANCE

- [ ] Every node has a row in the provenance table naming its source and its source class
- [ ] Nothing marked proposal or unknown is drawn as current behavior. Its status sits in its label, or it is left out
- [ ] Every causal edge is stated by its sources from both ends. An edge one source states and another contradicts is a finding, not a connector
- [ ] A contradicted item leaves a trace the reader can see. It sits in the reply's `Left out:` line with both sources and the reason, or the one question that asks which source governs settled it. Nothing is removed in silence and no extra line is invented for it

---

## 5. THE CHECK AND THE GATE

- [ ] `scripts/flow_check.py` printed `PASSED` for the model file, with the type each diagram was read as
- [ ] The measures printed beside the counts were read: the widest rank, the longest path, the connectors per step, the average label length and the crossing pairs, against the budgets `scripts/figjam_checks/layout.py` sets
- [ ] A measure out of band was fixed in the model rather than on the board and the check rerun after the change, because the composer owns the layout and a tangled shape is never rearranged after the write
- [ ] `scripts/compose_board.py` printed `COMPOSED` for every diagram, with the counts the read-back will look for
- [ ] The gate message names the plan, the file, what will be written, any planned extensions, the calls the write will spend and the rollback
- [ ] The gate showed the sketch with the check's result and answered the four critique questions `references/flow-mode.md` step 7 names, unless the user already settled them in this conversation
- [ ] On the generated fallback, an architecture call carries `useArchitectureLayoutCode`, and no other type carries it

---

## 6. THE BOARD

After the write, before the reply:

- [ ] The read-back counts match the model, as the type's reference sets them out
- [ ] Each provenance row whose class is not current behavior or whose edge is inferred was re-read against its source before the gate, and the row records the reason. A row that quotes a source line was not re-read
- [ ] The write returned no warning, and its counts match the counts the model expects
- [ ] The `COMPOSED` line named the design the board was drawn in, and each `DESIGN` warning it counted became a `Finding:` line naming the token and the shipped value the board used instead
- [ ] The overview is the screenshot the composing call returned, and `get_figjam` supplies the outline with a screenshot of each node
- [ ] A node that needs its own view is read with `get_screenshot` and a node id from that read, because the tool fails without one
- [ ] Two screenshots of the board were taken for this pass: one of the whole board in a single frame and one at 100% zoom. Composition is judged on the overview, because a crossing and a crowded label are invisible at reading size
- [ ] The overview reads in the order the model plans, and that order was written down before the first screenshot
- [ ] The overview shows no connector crossing another, no connector or label on a zone title, no two edges sharing a trunk the model draws apart and no two labels touching
- [ ] No edge runs through a zone it neither starts nor ends in. Edges that only arrive may share one magnet and then lie together for no more than 200 pixels
- [ ] One screenshot of the diagram shows no stretched shape, no label cut off and no overlap with existing board content
- [ ] Every gap a note or a person placed falls in one of the three bands `references/style-guide.md` Section 7 states, and two unrelated groups sit no closer than the text blocks inside a card
- [ ] Each zone holds its own nodes and no other, and no zone overlaps another
- [ ] The same screenshot shows no connector crossing and no edge that reads as joining the wrong node. Each edge is followed by eye from end to end, because a connector count does not prove that a route is clear
- [ ] Every colour on the board matches its entry in the key, the marked node sits where Section 3 places it, and the board answers the `userIntent` sentence without the model beside it
- [ ] Every fill on the board resolves to a role in the active design, as `assets/figjam-design.md` holds it, no zone tint shares a hue with a kind inside it or with the accent, and no note added a colour the design does not name
- [ ] The marked node reads first, and no other node competes with it, except on a state board, where it reads where the composer draws it and leads its glance line
- [ ] A screenshot finding is reported, and it is fixed only by reshaping the model and composing again after a yes, inside the two-attempt bound `references/flow-mode.md` Section 9 sets
- [ ] Each extension landed where planned and covers no composed node's label
- [ ] Nothing was moved, resized or restyled after the write
- [ ] Every finding below full marks names the label it sits on, where it sits in the frame, and one fix, which is a model change composed again after a yes or a named composer limit the writer cannot move

---

## 7. THE DESIGN RUBRIC

The checklists above decide whether a board may ship. The design rubric scores how well it reads, so two boards of the same model, or a board before and after a change, can be compared on something firmer than a glance. Score the overview screenshot on nine criteria, each 0, 1 or 2, for a total out of 18. A criterion scores 2 when it holds everywhere on the board, 1 when it holds with one named exception and 0 when it fails in two places or more.

| Criterion | Scores 2 when |
|---|---|
| Frame and entry | The board is one framed area with a title, a one-sentence subtitle and one obvious place to start reading |
| Reading order | The flow runs in one direction, the main route sits on one straight line and every branch sits beside it rather than across it |
| Colour by meaning | Every colour names a kind the key explains, and nothing is coloured for looks or by position |
| Grouping | Zones, lanes or composite states group what belongs together, each carries a visible name and neighbouring tints differ |
| Legibility | At overview zoom every label reads, no text is cut off or crowded and shapes of one kind share one size |
| Connector clarity | No connector crosses another or runs through a node or a zone title, two edges never lie on one stretch long enough to carry a label, every label sits on its own edge and clear of every other line and every end joins its node cleanly |
| Key and source | The key names every mark and nothing else, and the source line names the sources and what was left out |
| Proportion | The board reads wider than tall or close to square, with no tall strip, no large empty region and margins on the grid |
| Matches the active design | Every kind draws the pair its role names in `assets/figjam-design.md`, the title block and type sizes match every other board, the key lists its entries in the design's order with the focus last, every line takes the design's look and no zone tint shares a hue with a kind inside it |

Every score below 2 names the label or the zone it sits on and one fix, in the same shape Section 6 asks of a finding. A comparison between two boards scores both on the same nine criteria and reports both totals, criterion by criterion, so a gain on one criterion never hides a loss on another.

---

## 8. THE REPLY

- [ ] The board URL first, then the `Read-back:` line, then any `Extensions:` and `Left out:` lines, then any `Finding:` lines, then the `HVR self-scan:` line, with no text after it
- [ ] No sentence or key entry ties a colour or a zone tint to a team
- [ ] A mismatch is reported as measured, and the board is never called done on one
- [ ] No file was written to `export/`, and no Mermaid, HTML, SVG or PNG file was left behind
